## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll understand how every file on your computer is organized, what a file path actually means, and why this matters the moment you start working with code. None of this is complicated — it's just a mental model most people never get taught explicitly.

## The File System Is a Tree

Your computer organizes all its files in a **hierarchy** — think of it as an upside-down tree. At the very top (the root) is a drive, typically `C:\` on Windows. Every folder on your computer is a branch off that root, and every file is a leaf at the end of a branch.

Here's what that looks like:

```
C:\
├── Users\
│   └── Alice\
│       ├── Documents\
│       │   ├── Work\
│       │   └── Personal\
│       └── Desktop\
└── Program Files\
```

This structure — folders inside folders inside folders — is called a **directory tree**. The terms *folder* and *directory* mean the same thing; older documentation uses *directory*, modern interfaces use *folder*.

**Drives** are the top-level containers. Most Windows computers have one main drive called `C:`. If you plug in a USB stick or external hard drive, Windows assigns it another letter like `D:` or `E:`. The colon after the letter is how Windows signals "this is a drive." Everything starts from here.

## Anatomy of a File

Every file has four things that define it:

**Name** — The human-readable label, like `report` or `photo`.

**Extension** — The two-to-four letters after the dot that tell your computer *what kind of file this is*: `.txt` means plain text, `.jpg` means a photo, `.html` means a webpage, `.py` means a Python script. The extension is how Windows knows which program to open when you double-click a file.

**Path** — The full address of the file in the directory tree. More on this below.

**Icon** — The visual shortcut your computer uses to represent the file type. The icon is generated from the extension — it isn't stored in the file itself.

By default, Windows *hides* file extensions. This means `resume.docx` appears as just `resume`. This is unhelpful when you're learning to code, because the extension is crucial. Lesson 4-2 covers how to show extensions permanently.

## Paths: The Address of a File

A **path** is the full address that tells your computer exactly where a file lives. There are two types:

**Absolute path** — starts from the root of the drive and gives the complete location of a file, no matter where you currently are:
```
C:\Users\Alice\Documents\Work\report.docx
```
This is unambiguous. It will find the file from anywhere on the computer.

**Relative path** — describes a location *relative to where you currently are*. If you're already inside `C:\Users\Alice\Documents`, then the relative path to the same file is just:
```
Work\report.docx
```

Think of the difference this way: an **absolute path** is like a GPS address — it works from anywhere. A **relative path** is like saying "turn left, then the second door on the right" — it only makes sense if you already know where you're starting from.

**The backslash `\`** separates folders on Windows. You'll also see forward slashes `/` — that's the convention on Mac and Linux. Many tools accept either.

**The key insight for coding:** Code files are just files. When you write a program, you're creating text files in a folder. When that code references another file (an image, a stylesheet, a database), it uses a path to find it. If you get the path wrong, the file doesn't load. Understanding paths is not optional — it's one of the most practical skills in this entire course.

sections.title: Draw Your File Tree
sections.content:
Open Notepad (or any notes app) and draw the folder structure of your Documents folder as a tree. Follow this pattern:

```
Documents\
├── [Folder 1]\
│   ├── [Subfolder]\
│   └── [Another subfolder]\
├── [Folder 2]\
└── [Folder 3]\
    └── [File inside it]
```

Don't worry about getting every folder — just the ones you actually use and recognise.

Then, write the **absolute path** to one specific file inside your Documents folder. It should look something like:
```
C:\Users\YourName\Documents\SomeFolder\SomeFile.docx
```

Finally, write one sentence answering: *"Why does a coder need to understand file paths?"*

Save this — it's the foundation everything in Parts 4 and 5 builds on.

sections.question: What is the difference between an absolute path and a relative path?
options: An absolute path starts from the drive root and works from anywhere; a relative path describes a location from where you currently are
An absolute path uses backslashes; a relative path uses forward slashes
An absolute path is for files; a relative path is for folders
An absolute path is longer; a relative path is shorter
sections.explanation: An absolute path always starts from the root (like C:\) and unambiguously identifies a file from anywhere on the computer. A relative path only makes sense in the context of a current location — it describes how to get to a file from where you already are.
